vignette:
Captain Katarina's Story

Katarina Novak had commanded container ships across the Atlantic for thirty-eight years, and in all that time, she had never once called in sick. Even after her husband, Dmitri, died seven years ago, she kept to her schedule with the same meticulous discipline she brought to navigation and crew management. At seventy-six, with silver hair pulled back in the same tight bun she'd worn since her twenties, she remained the oldest active captain in her shipping company's fleet—a distinction she wore like a medal. But last October, everything changed.

She had been docked in Baltimore, overseeing the unloading of a cargo vessel, when a routine dispute between two dock workers escalated. One man, enraged, began shouting at a supervisor. Katarina, seeing the situation spiraling, moved to intervene as she always did. Within seconds, police arrived—two officers in dark uniforms who moved toward the agitated worker with hands already on their belts. What happened next unfolded in fragments that would never leave her: the officer's rigid posture, the sudden movement, the man on the ground, the officer's boot, the sounds. Katarina had stepped forward to say something—she could no longer remember what—and the second officer had turned to her, his hand raised, his face contorted. He had not struck her, but he had shoved her backward against a steel container with enough force to knock the wind from her lungs. She was seventy-six years old. She had been trying to help. The officer had looked at her with something like contempt before turning back to his partner.

In the weeks that followed, Katarina discovered that her mind had recorded every detail with a clarity that felt almost photographic. When she closed her eyes—and increasingly, even when she didn't—she could see the officer's face with perfect precision: the exact shade of his skin, the texture of his uniform, the angle of his jaw as he shoved her. The memory was not like remembering; it was like the event was still happening, unfolding in real time behind her eyes. She would be standing on the bridge of her ship, reviewing cargo manifests, and suddenly she was back on that dock, her chest compressed against cold steel, her breath stolen, the weight of his hand on her shoulder blade.

The vividness of these memories terrified her. She had come to believe that if she stopped moving, if she allowed herself even a moment of stillness, the images would consume her entirely. So she threw herself into work with an intensity that alarmed her first mate. She arrived at the dock hours before her crew, stayed long after they left, and volunteered for additional voyages. She reorganized her entire filing system, rewrote operational manuals that had served perfectly well for years, and began taking on administrative tasks that had nothing to do with her role. Her colleagues noticed but said nothing; Katarina Novak was legendary for her work ethic, and besides, what did they know of what she carried?

But the more she worked, the more the memories demanded her attention. The constant activity—the endless tasks she invented to fill her waking hours—seemed only to sharpen the photographic quality of her recollections. In the quiet moments between tasks, when she paused to take a breath or review what she had accomplished, the images returned with even greater force, as though her mind had been storing them up, waiting for any lapse in her vigilance. She found herself ruminating endlessly about why this had happened to her, what she could have done differently, whether she had somehow provoked the officer's rage. She dwelled, too, on who she had been before—the woman who could walk onto a dock without fear, who could intervene in a conflict without calculating the cost, who had never questioned her own safety in the spaces she had commanded for nearly four decades.

The overwork had begun to have consequences she could no longer ignore. She had made a navigation error last month, a small one, caught by her first mate before it mattered. She had never made navigation errors. Her crew, sensing something was wrong, had grown cautious around her. The company had begun to ask questions. And Katarina, sitting alone in her captain's quarters on her last voyage, had finally admitted to herself that she could not outrun what had happened. She had come to seek help not because she believed it would work, but because she was terrified of what would happen if she did not—of losing the one thing that still felt like hers: her reputation, her competence, the identity she had spent a lifetime building.
